rubric.item: AC#3 audit completeness (justified budgets left alone)

findings.issue: The AC#3 audit leaves the 400-slice conditional loops as 'justified: condition-bounded; 400 slices take several real seconds' (spec section 5 clock table, last row). This task's own measurement contradicts that: blocked-1.resolved.json records 1,200 slices of 50 ms in 3,105 ms real on WebKit (~2.6 ms/slice), so 400 slices are ~1 s real. These loops are still bounded by fake time (20,000 ms) while waiting on real-time worker replies, which is the same race class this task removes. The most exposed sites are the fold-to-end-of-hand loops (action-bar.spec.ts:177-179 on the second context, action-bar.spec.ts:243-246, table.spec.ts nextTurnPaused at :124, next-hand/review slicesUntil). They have to absorb every remaining bot reply of a hand. After the bot step timers use their fake time, only a few hundred slices (well under 1 s real) are left for all of those replies combined. With delayWorkerReplies(2000), these loops would fail just like the old 1,000 ms budget did.
findings.evidence: doit/TASK-1.52/blocked-1.resolved.json evidence: 'not my turn after 60000 ms fake / 3105 ms real (WebKit)'. spec.md section 5 row: '400-slice conditional loops ... condition-bounded; 400 slices take several real seconds | justified'. e2e/action-bar.spec.ts:177 `for (let slice = 0; slice < 400 && (await handOver(real).count()) === 0; slice++) await real.clock.runFor(50);`
findings.fix: Correct the audit: either (a) measure the real duration of each 400-slice loop (log Date.now() deltas on CI or locally) and replace the 'several real seconds' justification in the audit (task implementation notes) with the measured real budget and the margin over normal reply latency, escalating if the margin is under about 5x; or (b), as a follow-up task with the owners' unlock approval, give these loops a real-time bound too (for example a predicate variant of runUntilMyTurn). Do not leave a justification that the task's own data disproves.

findings.issue: SPEC-07 only exercises the real-time bound (maxRealMs: 500). The maxFakeMs branch is never hit by a test. The spec does not require it, and the logic is a single shared condition.
findings.evidence: runUntilMyTurn(page, { maxRealMs: 500 }) with default maxFakeMs 600,000 trips on real time after ~190 slices.
findings.fix: Optional: add `runUntilMyTurn(page, { maxFakeMs: 100 })` to the same test, expecting the same message prefix.

findings.issue: The old 1,000 ms budgets also implied 'my turn arrives within 1 s of fake time'. With maxFakeMs 600,000, a bot-delay regression (say, seconds per bot step) would no longer fail these six specs. This is acceptable because rapid-pace.spec.ts (:218, :249, :274, :292) asserts bot pacing directly, and the A-3 deviation is sound: 60,000 fake ms is used up in ~3 s real, before SPEC-04's ≥4 s of delayed replies arrive. Noted for the record only.
findings.evidence: maxFakeMs = 600_000; rapid-pace.spec.ts 'each bot action at 6-max shows within 300 ms of the previous action'.

summary: Implementation matches the spec. Unit versions keep every expect (lineUpPolicyFactory at 20/100/20 hands runs 1.7 s locally under coverage, and Tough still differs from all-TAG). Both moved tests match the base commit verbatim in their new acceptance files (checked with diff). The calling-station unit file keeps the stub block unchanged. In all six locked e2e files, only the clock-advance lines, imports and the now-unused runFor1000/toActSeats changed; no expect was added, removed or loosened. runUntilMyTurn checks before every slice, so at most one 50 ms slice runs after the turn arrives, and the user's turn starts no timer. Nothing timer-driven that a test later asserts is skipped. It throws on either bound, and the 10 s real bound sits inside the 30 s test timeout. The recorded maxFakeMs 600,000 deviation is justified. delayWorkerReplies matches the design, and the SPEC-05 control fails if the delay is a no-op, so it genuinely reproduces the race. worker-delay + action-bar-limits: 12/12 passed on both engines (7.7 s). One MAJOR: the audit's justification for the remaining 400-slice loops ('several real seconds') is contradicted by the task's own ~2.6 ms/slice measurement (~1 s real), so those loops still carry the same worker-vs-fake-clock race with only more margin.
